description: 🚀 Nanhu Space Club is a team of builders passionate about space, AI, software, data, and game development. We love turning ambitious ideas into working prototypes using NASA’s open data. Looking for curious, driven teammates in astronomy, aerospace, ML/AI, Python, GIS, UI/UX, 3D/game development, hardware, and science communication. If you want to build something bold, learn fast, and aim high—join us!
summary:
NANHU-1: The Journey is a cinematic browser-based lunar exploration game by Nanhu Space Club. Players lead an autonomous rover mission to the Moon’s south pole, balancing scientific discovery with safety, power, communication and a 26-kilogram equipment limit.

The mission begins with a conversation between Nanhu and a senior scientist. An active-speaker lighting system highlights the scientist in warm amber and Nanhu in cool blue. Players then choose a NASA-derived landing region, scientific instruments, power system, communication method and mission priority.

After launch and landing, players manually drive the rover or use autopilot routes to visit scientific stations. Six instruments—including a spectrometer, ground-penetrating radar and drill—collect different types of evidence. Decisions affect battery level, rover integrity, communications, scientific value and the final score.

The mission can end in a safe return, heroic rover loss or extraordinary preliminary discovery. The game emphasizes responsible science by requiring independent measurements before interpreting a signal as possible lunar water ice.

Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js and Zustand, NANHU-1 includes 3D environments, recorded dialogue, captions, checkpoints, accessibility settings and deterministic outcomes.
details:
What does the project do?

NANHU-1: The Journey is an interactive 3D game in which the player directs a fictional robotic expedition

to the lunar south pole. The story follows Nanhu, a mission director on Earth, and a senior mission

scientist. Players choose a landing region, scientific instruments, power system, communication link and

mission priority. Their choices affect the rover’s mass, available energy, scientific capability and final

outcome.

The experience combines a cinematic launch and Earth parking orbit with a translunar coast, lunar

landing and hands-on surface exploration. On the Moon, players drive or use autonomous routes,

approach science stations, operate instruments and interpret simulated observations. They must

balance evidence collection against battery reserve, vehicle condition, communications and the

possibility of losing the rover.

How does it work?

The browser renders a Three.js 3D world behind a React interface. A mission state machine controls

seven narrative acts, branching decisions, checkpoints, dialogue and endings. A bounded 60 Hz

simulation updates driving and resources. NASA LRO/LOLA elevation crops define four separate surface

meshes and supply the same height samples used for rover attitude, ground clearance and

terrain-aware effects.

Each of the six payload instruments has its own acquisition animation and a timed measurement.

Results are stored as readings, contribute to a science score and influence later choices. The player can

return with a safer but smaller result or continue investigating at greater risk. Instrument readings and

discovery outcomes are authored game scenarios; the elevation data do not establish actual ice

deposits.

Why NASA data matter to this game

NASA data are part of the playable environment, not just background decoration. The four elevation

crops directly shape the ground over which the rover moves. NASA Earth and Moon models provide

planetary context, while historical spacecraft assets and archival launch audio connect the fictional story

with real spaceflight heritage. Source records identify each asset, its treatment and its limitations.

What is measured data, and what is illustrative?

Measured-source content: NASA-derived elevation grids, their coordinate reference systems and the

source geometry/textures of imported NASA models. Generated content: rock placement, fine crater

materials, dust particles, vehicles built in code, station locations, route layouts, shadow-zone graphics,

sunlight ratings, instrument readings and mission dialogue.

The four maps are 600 × 650 m patches at 5 m grid spacing and 1× vertical scale. They are not

complete reconstructions of the named craters and are not NASA-certified landing sites. Interpolated

source pixels and varying spatial uncertainty limit what can be inferred from the terrain. Hydration or

hydrogen-sensitive evidence alone is not proof of accessible water ice.

Intended benefits and impact

The project aims to make lunar mission planning understandable through consequences rather than a

list of facts. Players experience why an additional instrument consumes mass and energy, why

communication strategy matters, and why several independent measurements are more informative

than a single promising signal. The intended audiences are students, space-club visitors and people

exploring planetary science for the first time.

Its intended impact is greater curiosity about NASA open data and more careful reasoning about

scientific uncertainty. These are design goals, not measured learning outcomes. A future classroom

study could compare pre/post understanding of mission trade-offs, track completion rates and test

whether players distinguish simulated readings from real terrain observations.

How the project is creative

The game combines a character-led story with a configurable engineering problem. Players do not

simply travel through a fixed animation: their payload and risk decisions alter what evidence they can

collect and how the mission ends. A rotating globe connects a named landing choice to its mapped

terrain. Distinct instrument mechanisms make scientific work visible, while locally bundled voices,

captions and an animated cover support the narrative.

NASA data are adapted into a playable landscape, while original procedural rocks and regolith add visual

detail without overwriting the source elevations. The rocket and lander sequences link launch, orbital

coast and lunar operations into one experience. This combination of data, narrative and decision-based

learning is the central creative contribution.
